newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Primakov calls for sanctions on Estonia.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Primakov calls for sanctions on Estonia.

text.p: Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Thursday that Russia should impose economic sanctions on countries discriminating against ethnic Russians and singled out Estonia, Itar-Tass news agency said.
Primakov, addressing a cabinet meeting, mentioned the Baltic former Soviet republic among those countries where he thought Russia should act to protect Russian speakers.
"Russia should not be afraid to use economic sanctions (in such cases)," Tass quoted Primakov as saying.
Urging the cabinet to impose sanctions against Estonia, Tass said Primakov, a former spy chief, told the meeting about 60 percent of Estonia's national revenue originated from trade with Russia.

"We keep pressurising Estonia on humanitarian issues (we want it) at least to fulfil recommendations by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe on the treatment of Russian speakers in this republic," Primakov said.
Western countries have advised Estonia and fellow Baltic state Latvia to do more for their Russian communities to pave their way into international organisations they want to join, including NATO.
Hundreds of thousands of Russian speakers were stranded in Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia after they regained independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.

Most Russians living in Latvia and Estonia do not have citizenship and say they had been shut out of political life. Many of them are deeply nostalgic for the past when they felt secure in the Soviet empire.
In Lithuania, where the Russian community is much smaller, all ethnic Russians were given citizenship.
Russia's State duma lower house of parliament accused Latvia late last year of violating the rights of ethnic Russians and also called for economic sanctions to be imposed.

In 1995 Primakov's soft-spoken predecessor Andrei Kozyrev threatened to use military force to protect Russians living in former Soviet republics, drawing a wave of surprise and alarm from the Baltic region.
Primakov also said the government should take steps to create conditions to allow Russian communities to live abroad instead of moving them back to Russia.
